questions.q: In the Python MCP SDK's @mcp.tool() pattern, how does the SDK generate a tool's schema and description?
options: From the function's type hints and its docstring
You must hand-write a separate JSON Schema file for every tool
The SDK guesses randomly and you correct it afterward
Schemas cannot be generated automatically; this is not supported
questions.explain: The MCPServer class reads Python type hints (e.g. latitude: float) and the function's docstring to automatically generate the tool's inputSchema and description.

questions.q: Why does a poorly written docstring still produce a weak tool, even with the SDK auto-generating the schema?
options: It doesn't matter at all what the docstring says
The SDK ignores docstrings entirely
Docstrings are not allowed in MCP tools
The SDK is only as good as the docstring you give it — a vague docstring produces a vague generated description, the same issue as a hand-written one
questions.explain: Automatic generation doesn't remove the need for a clear, specific docstring — it just moves where that description comes from. The underlying quality bar from the tool-schema lesson still applies.

questions.q: What happens if a stdio-based MCP server's code calls Python's print()?
options: Nothing — print() is always safe to use
It writes to stdout, which corrupts the JSON-RPC messages on that same channel and breaks the server
It automatically gets redirected to a log file
It only causes a problem for HTTP-based servers, never stdio ones
questions.explain: stdio uses standard input/output as the actual protocol message channel. print() writes to stdout by default, corrupting the JSON-RPC stream the client is trying to parse.

questions.q: What is the correct way to log inside a stdio-based MCP server?
options: Use print() exclusively
Logging is not possible in a stdio server
Use the standard logging module, which writes to stderr by default, leaving stdout clean for protocol messages
Write log messages directly into the tool's return value
questions.explain: The logging module writes to stderr, not stdout, so it never interferes with the JSON-RPC messages flowing over stdio.

questions.q: Per this lesson's scoping guidance, what's the first question to ask before adding a new capability to a server you're building?
options: How many total lines of code will it require?
Whether it should actually be exposed as a tool (model-controlled action) or would fit better as a resource (application-controlled, read-only context)
Whether it will make the server file longer than 1000 lines
Whether the capability can be written in a language other than Python
questions.explain: This connects directly back to the tools-vs-resources distinction: not everything you expose from a server should be a tool just because it's convenient to add a decorator to a function.
